notes.3i: Many good diagrams of planar structures were seen here. This was often done using no 3D bonds at all. Other correct renditions were seen that used the 3D bond conventions accurately. Some non-planar structures, some of them pyramidal and some of them tetrahedral, were also seen.
notes.3ii: The best answers made it clear that the cis-platin binds to the DNA in the cells and that the consequence is that the cells involved are unable to undergo cell division. An alternative to the second part is that cis-platin binding to the DNA will prevent DNA replication. Some answers were seen that referred to preventing the spread of cancer, or the killing of tumour cells, which did not go far enough to gain credit.
notes.3iii: This was generally answered well. Many candidates understood that use of the [O] convention requires the balancing of the equation for oxygen atoms.
notes.3iv: Most of the candidates who deduced B = CoCO were able to go on to write an ionic equation for reaction 3.
notes.3d: Accurate copying of the structure of the cyclobutane-1,1-carboxylate ligand was necessary and this accuracy was seen on many scripts.

notes.5b: Many candidates found this calculation challenging. However, correct working out was seen on many scripts, so that it was often possible to award partial credit in some cases. Some candidates explained clearly in words what each step in their calculation meant. It was easier to understand the candidate’s purpose and to award credit in such cases. An example of this approach involves describing each line of the calculation as: 1. moles of Ce4+ in 21.8cm3 2. moles of NO – that reacted with this 3. moles of NO – in the 100cm3 in the volumetric flask 4. mass of NaNO in the 100cm3 in the volumetric flask 5. purity of NaNO . An approach like this might also have helped candidates to think clearly and to find their way through this calculation.
notes.5i: The information in the question, ‘The reagent used is a copper(I) salt’ was often missed. Many answers such as HCN and NaCN were seen.
notes.5ii: Approximately equal numbers of candidates appreciated that reaction 2 is hydrolysis of the nitrile group and that reaction 3 is oxidation of the methyl groups on the ring.
notes.5g: Candidates found this question very demanding.
notes.6i: It was rare to see the correct amide product here. Many answers were seen that involved impossible rearrangements, or that did not match the given molecular formula. More candidates were able to draw a correct structure formed when the S they had drawn was treated with LiAlH . An example of this was the drawing of S with an aldehyde group. This did not gain credit for S, but if T was then drawn with the aldehyde group reduced correctly to a primary alcohol group, credit for T could be awarded.
notes.6ii: ‘Condensation’ was rarely seen for step I but many candidates identified step II as ‘reduction’.
notes.6c: Candidates should be warned that drawing a section of a polymer chain using skeletal formulae involves extra care. The ‘continuation bonds’ (i.e. the bonds to the neighbouring monomer residues) can easily be ambiguous, as they could either be continuation bonds or they could be methyl groups. Candidates who chose to use structural or displayed formulae did not encounter this difficulty.
notes.7ii: Many candidates used the information provided correctly to produce an accurate diagram of the repeat unit of the polyurethane LycraⓇ. No credit was given for copying the diagram of ‘a polyurethane’ at the top of the page.
notes.7iii: The presence of hydrogen bonding in a structure such as LycraⓇ was deduced by a minority of candidates.

notes.8i: This was generally answered well. (ii, iii and iv) More candidates now appreciate that when using the Gibbs equation, care is needed with units, as ∆H is given in kJ mol–1 while ∆S is given in J mol–1. A number of wrong renditions of the Gibbs equation were seen.
notes.8ii: A common error for hybridisation was sp2.
notes.8v: Since ∆S is negative as T increases, T∆S becomes a greater negative number. Alternatively, as T increases –T∆S becomes a greater positive number.
notes.8d: Many good answers were seen. This question required good chemistry, careful use of words and specific vocabulary. An example of this use of specific vocabulary can be seen in the marking point for recognising that basicity depends on the tendency of the lone pair to be protonated. It was also correct for a candidate to write that basicity depends on the tendency of the lone pair to receive a proton. By contrast, expressions such as ‘basicity depends on the tendency of a substance to be attacked by a proton’ were not accepted. A few candidates assumed the question was about differences in acidity.
notes.9b: Candidates found this question challenging. The significance of the buffer pH being so close to the isoelectric point of cysteine and the consequent likelihood that cysteine molecules would exist in an uncharged state, was not often appreciated. Many candidates were able to deduce that glutamic acid will travel further than the dipeptide but were not able to go on to explain this answer clearly by reference to molecular mass. CHEMISTRY
notes.key_messages: • Candidates should avoid the early rounding of intermediate answers during calculations. • Candidates are reminded that observations for a chemical reaction should focus on the physical changes that take place. • The use of the Data Booklet should be encouraged for questions involving infra-red spectra. • When a question asks for a name of a reagent(s) then the formula of reagent(s) is not acceptable. General comments
notes.general_comments: General comments The majority of candidates were able to finish the paper within the hour allowed. Questions 1, 21, 30, 34 and 39 were found to be more challenging to candidates. Comments on specific question The most commonly chosen incorrect answer was C. From the Data Booklet the element is gallium. When three electrons have been removed, the electronic configuration of the Ga3+ ion is 1s22s22p63s23p63d10. The third shell is full at this point.
